items.summary_raw:

Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

As a result of the strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.

Water companies in the UK made more than £340m in revenue last year by pouring billions of litres of industrial and commercial wastewater into sewage treatment works that experts say are not designed to remove most chemicals, leaving pollutants to pass into rivers, seas and farmland.

Water companies are required by law to take industrial wastewater and issue permits called “trade-effluent consents” that allow businesses to send it to sewage works, though water companies can refuse applications.

items.title: MoD has objected to four windfarms in past year over radar interference fears
items.summary_raw:
Complaints risks putting defence ministry on collision course with Department for Energy Security and Net Zero

The Ministry of Defence has objected to at least four planned windfarms in the past year over fears the spinning blades could cause “unacceptable interference” with radars used to detect military aircraft.

MoD officials raised concerns in late June over plans for an onshore windfarm in County Durham that could result in aircraft “not being detected” within an RAF Low Flying Area, according to a letter to Britain’s planning authority.

Iran will not abandon uranium enrichment or hand over its uranium, the head of the country's Atomic Energy Organisation, Mohammad Eslami, said on Thursday.

Eslami said new US threats against Iran's nuclear sites were "nothing new" and that enrichment was "an inseparable part" of the nuclear process, state media reported.

Turkey is assessing how it can help Saudi Arabia defend against attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi movement under a joint defence pact with Pakistan, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Thursday, ruling out Turkish participation in offensive operations.

Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all. The three countries have since held political and military meetings following Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, with the countries agreeing on Monday to immediately implement their collective defence commitments and ensure the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.

items.title: Trump says deal with Iran 'isn't really something that I want to do'
items.summary_raw:
Trump says deal with Iran 'isn't really something that I want to do'

US President Donald Trump said that his special envoy Steve Witkoff is "doing very well" in discussions with Iran, but added that a deal with Tehran is not his preferred outcome.

"He's working on the Iran deal and doing very well. I think the deal isn't really something that I want to do, but they're willing to offer us anything to stop," Trump said during a campaign rally in Texas.

"They will never have a nuclear weapon," he added.

The US president also expressed that he expects the war on Iran to end soon, saying: "That war ends - it's going to be very soon. It's got to be very soon," he said, describing Iran as "a failed nation."

items.title: World must change way it produces food to avoid biodiversity collapse, says WWF
items.summary_raw:
Recovery of tigers, tuna and green sea turtles show nature loss can be reversed when action taken, charity says

Conservation comebacks for wild tigers, tuna and green​ sea turtles prove that global nature loss can be reversed, ​scientists have said. ​But a report warns food production must be the next ​“positive tipping point​” if the world is to avert biodiversity collapse.

The World Wildlife Fund (WWF) analysed nearly 36,000 animal populations and more than 5,000 species, producing the largest ever database of vertebrate wildlife. Scientists found populations had declined by an average of 73% since 1970, showing that “nature continues to be degraded at an alarming scale”, with “no sign of losses slowing”.

items.title: Heatstroke ruined his health. Years before, it took the life of another farm worker at the same company
items.summary_raw:
A farm labor contractor exposed laborers on H-2A agricultural visas to heat-related health hazards, but is still bringing hundreds of migrant farm workers to North Carolina

It was 4pm and 90F (32C) when Carlos Vargas Moreno and other farm workers set out to weed a watermelon field in Goldsboro, North Carolina, on 19 July 2022.

The work day had begun at 7am and included two 15-minute breaks and a one-hour lunch eaten outdoors. The heat index – what the temperature feels like to the human body when relative humidity is combined with the air temperature – was 98.3F. It was the kind of day that a heat safety app created by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (Osha) and the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (Niosh) defined as “hazardous” for outdoor workers.

items.title: During last night's large-scale Russian missile attack on Ukraine, the interception rate of Kh-101 cruise missiles was unusually low - one of the lowest so far this year.   Out of …
items.summary_raw: During last night's large-scale Russian missile attack on Ukraine, the interception rate of Kh-101 cruise missiles was unusually low - one of the lowest so far this year.   Out of roughly 48 Kh-101 cruise missiles launched, I could only confirm around 10 interceptions, mainly by fighter jets.   In my opinion, this was caused by Ukraine's ongoing F-16 maintenance crisis, and due to the fact that Russia is striking areas of Ukraine closer to the border, providing Ukrainian air defences with much less time to shoot down the missiles. The missiles also flew in very large groups immediately towards their targets, without changing course much, completely overwhelming Ukrainian air defences.   The Kh-101s impacted three cities - Kremenchuk (Poltava Oblast), Pryluky (Chernihiv Oblast), and Oleksandriya (Kirovohrad Oblast).  Most of the impacts occurred in Kremenchuk, while around a dozen occurred in Oleksandriya, along with another dozen or so in Pryluky. Multiple different locations in Kremenchuk, including the hydroelectric power plant, were hit. NICOSIA – The government in Nicosia neither confirmed nor denied a report in the newspaper Phileleftheros that President Nikos Christodoulides has submitted a proposal to open Varosha under UN administration in exchange for the operation of the port of Famagusta under EU supervision. The director of the President’s Press Office, Victoras Papadopoulos, in statements to the state broadcaster RIK, confined himself to recalling that President Christodoulides had submitted 19 proposals on different issues during the leaders’ last meeting, on September 17, the contents of which, he said, he could not disclose in order to protect the peace effort currently underway. Even the mayor of occupied Famagusta, Simos Ioannou, said he was unaware that such a proposal had been submitted, stressing, however, that he had long been asking the government to submit a proposal for Varosha and that the President had committed to doing so at a meeting held approximately two months ago.

items.title: Marco Rubio in Athens for U.S.-Greece Strategic Dialogue: Defense, energy, regional security high on the agenda
items.summary_raw:
ATHENS - U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in Athens late Tuesday for the sixth round of the U.S.-Greece Strategic Dialogue, landing at Athens International Airport at approximately 9:20 p.m. and being received by Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis. Rubio’s visit comes as the two allies seek to further deepen their cooperation in defense, energy and regional security, with the agenda also covering shipping, technology, trade and investment. Before arriving in Athens, Rubio described Greece as a “very important ally” of the United States. On defense, particular emphasis is expected to be placed on further strengthening U.S.-Greek military cooperation, including the F-35 program and the upgrade of Greece’s F-16 fleet to the Viper configuration. The talks are also expected to address the procurement of additional U.S. weapons systems and support for existing American-made equipment operated by the Greek armed forces.

items.title: Agreement to transition away from fossil fuels ‘not open for renegotiation’, Pacific leader tells pre-Cop
items.summary_raw:
International leaders visit Tuvalu as part of climate talks co-hosted by Australia ahead of Cop31 conference

Pacific island leaders have urged a promised global transition away from fossil fuels must not be left open to renegotiation as they gather in tiny Tuvalu in a bid to build momentum before a major climate summit.

About 50 dignitaries – 14 national heads including Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, a list of climate change ministers and the heads of global agencies – flew to the low-lying atoll nation in a bid to bring attention to the plight of the countries most at risk from the climate crisis.

items.title: US supreme court to hear big oil’s bid to block climate damage lawsuits
items.summary_raw:
Court starts new term hearing Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil’s attempt to stop lawsuits at state level

The US supreme court begins its new nine-month term hearing arguments Monday in a high-stakes case in which big oil companies are attempting to strike a fatal blow against lawsuits that seek to hold them accountable for the climate crisis.

In Suncor Energy versus the County Commissioners of Boulder County, local officials in Boulder are suing Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil in state court to force the companies to share a portion of the costs that climate change has imposed on local taxpayers. However, Exxon and Canada-based Suncor are arguing that federal law prevents state courts from hearing Boulder’s climate change lawsuit.

Australia had its second hottest September on record last month as global heating and a strengthening El Niño combined to break a string of heat records around the country.

Bureau of Meteorology data showed the minimum night-time temperatures across the continent were also the hottest for any September, on a record that goes back to 1910. Averaged temperatures ranked in the top five warmest Septembers for every state, and the sixth hottest for the Northern Territory.

items.title: Australia and Turkey criticised for hosting UN climate conference while embracing coal
items.summary_raw:
Global campaign group 350.org urges Cop31 hosts to announce a coal phase-out date and national roadmaps to get off fossil fuels

  • Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter here

The hosts of the next major United Nations climate conference, Turkey and Australia, are facing criticism for being partners in a coal supply chain while remaining near silent on the need for a global deal to rapidly get off fossil fuels.

With the Cop31 summit in the Turkish Mediterranean city of Antalya just a month away, the two countries running the fortnight-long talks have been accused by activists of a “vacuum of action” on plans for a transition away from coal, gas and oil – a key goal of many nations at the talks.

items.title: The expansion of Heathrow would be an expensive disaster for Britain and the world. Burnham needs to block it | George Monbiot
items.summary_raw:
A third runway would fly in the face of reason. If we are to prioritise human life over short-term ‘growth’, we need to use planes less, not more


If a third runway is built at Heathrow, what will be the impact on the wealth of the nation? It will cost us somewhere between £23.4bn and £62.5bn. These are not my figures; they weren’t calculated by environmental groups, but by the Department for Transport.

For decades, government ministers have told us that airport expansion is essential for “growth”. As chancellor, Rachel Reeves claimed that a third runway at Heathrow would add 0.43% to GDP, figures we later discovered came from a report commissioned by the airport.
